followUps:
AOT (ahead-of-time) compilation turns your templates into plain JavaScript at build time, so the browser never has to compile them.

The alternative, JIT, shipped the compiler to the user and compiled in the browser. AOT gives a smaller bundle (no compiler, around 100 KB less), faster startup, template errors caught at build time, and better tree-shaking because the compiler sees exactly which code is used. Since Ivy it is the default for ng build and ng serve.

Register it in the app config with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...])), so it applies to every request made through HttpClient.

export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) =>
  next(req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token } }));

provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor]))

Requests are immutable, so you clone. Interceptors run in the order listed on the way out, and in reverse on the way back. Use them for auth headers, logging and error handling. In module apps you provide HTTP_INTERCEPTORS instead.

Without Zone.js, Angular no longer re-checks the tree after every async event; it only re-renders when something tells it to.

Triggers become: a signal read in a template changing, a template event listener firing, markForCheck, the async pipe emitting, or a component being created or destroyed. You add provideZonelessChangeDetection() and remove the zone.js polyfill, which shrinks the bundle and gives cleaner stack traces. Code that relied on a plain field being changed inside a setTimeout will stop updating unless that field is a signal.

Point a route at it with loadComponent and a dynamic import(). The bundler splits that file into its own chunk, downloaded only when the route is visited.

{ path: 'admin',
  loadComponent: () => import('./admin').then(m => m.Admin) }

For a whole feature use loadChildren with a routes array. Inside a template, @defer lazy loads a standalone component without any route.

Providers go in the application config (bootstrapApplication(App, { providers: [...] })), in a route's providers array, or in a component's own providers.

Most services simply use @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }), needing no registration. Route-level providers create an environment injector for that route and its children, so a service there lives only while the route is active (a feature-scoped store, for example). Component providers give one instance per component instance.

Yes. List the NgModule in the standalone component's imports array, and everything that module exports becomes usable in the template.

For example, importing MatButtonModule or a legacy SharedModule works directly. The reverse also works: an NgModule can import a standalone component in its imports, not its declarations. That is what allows migrating one component at a time. A standalone component can never be listed in declarations; Angular reports an error.

An HTML attribute is the text written in the markup and only sets the initial value; a DOM property is the live value on the element object.

Example: <input value="Ann">. After the user types "Bob", the attribute still says "Ann" but input.value is "Bob". Angular property binding [value] sets the property, which is why it follows the current state. Some attributes have no property (aria-*), so use [attr.aria-label].

Declare an input called value and an output called valueChange; the banana-in-a-box syntax matches them by name.

value = input(0);
valueChange = output<number>();
inc() { this.valueChange.emit(this.value() + 1); }
// modern: value = model(0); value.set(5)

The parent writes [(value)]="count", which expands to [value]="count" (valueChange)="count = $event". model() creates both in one line and gives a writable signal.

Because templates are re-run very often and must stay fast, predictable and safe, so they cannot do anything that changes state or escapes the component.

No assignment operators in expressions (except in event handlers), no new, no ++, no globals like window or Math, and no chained statements. This keeps change detection free of side effects: calling an expression twice, as dev mode does, gives the same result. Complex logic belongs in a computed or method instead.

code.title: @for track: reuse rows by key vs by index

followUps:
track tells Angular which old row belongs to which item, so it can reuse and move DOM nodes instead of rebuilding them.

With track item.id, a reorder just moves existing rows. With track $index, row 0 stays row 0, so after a reorder every row is rewritten with new data, and any state inside them (input text, focus, animations) sticks to the position, not the item. Use $index only for static lists that never reorder or insert. The program above shows 3 rewrites versus 0.

@defer loads a block of the template, and its component dependencies, lazily in a separate chunk, when a trigger fires.

Triggers: on idle (default), on viewport, on interaction, on hover, on immediate, on timer(2s), and when expr for a custom condition. Add @placeholder, @loading and @error blocks for the states. prefetch on ... downloads early but renders later. It is ideal for heavy charts or below-the-fold content.

@if removes the elements and destroys the components inside, while [hidden] only hides them with CSS.

With @if (open) turned false, child components run ngOnDestroy, their local state is lost, subscriptions are cleaned, and turning it true builds everything again. With [hidden] the nodes stay alive and keep running change detection and timers. Use @if for heavy or stateful content; use hiding when toggling is frequent and you want to keep scroll or form state.

Use a shared service when the two components are far apart in the tree, or when many components need the same state.

Passing inputs through four levels ("prop drilling") is noisy; a root or route-scoped service holding a signal lets any component read and update it. Example: a cart with 3 items shown in the header, a list page and checkout. Keep inputs and outputs for direct parent-child pairs, since they are explicit and easy to test; reach for a service when the data has its own lifecycle.

Because the object belongs to the parent, and changing it silently changes the parent's data without the parent knowing.

If a child does item().qty++, the parent's array is altered, other components showing it may not refresh, and OnPush will not notice since the reference is the same. The correct way is to emit an event, qtyChange.emit(3), and let the owner create a new object: items = items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, qty: 3 } : i). Data down, events up.

Content projection lets a parent pass markup into a child's template, shown where the child places <ng-content>.

A card component with <ng-content select="[title]"></ng-content> and a default <ng-content> can be used as <app-card><h2 title>Hi</h2>Body</app-card>. The projected elements are created and owned by the parent. The child can read them with contentChild(). It is the Angular version of "slots" or React's children.

Read the input inside a computed() or an effect(), because signal inputs are signals.

id = input.required<number>();
user = computed(() => this.store.byId(this.id()));
constructor() {
  effect(() => console.log('id is', this.id()));
}

When the parent changes the bound value from 4 to 5, user is recalculated and the effect runs once. For loading data, resource() or rxResource() can be driven by the input. This replaces ngOnChanges and setter inputs.

input() is read-only for the child; model() is a writable signal that also sends changes back to the parent.

With input(0) the child can only read count(). With model(0) the child can call count.set(5), and Angular emits countChange, so a parent using [(count)]="n" sees 5. Use input for data the parent controls and model only for real two-way things like a custom checkbox or slider.

linkedSignal creates a writable signal that resets itself whenever another signal changes.

Classic problem: a dropdown's selected option should default to the first item, the user may change it, but when the option list changes it should reset. selected = linkedSignal(() => this.options()[0]) gives the first option, lets you call selected.set(x), and recomputes if options changes. Without it you would need an effect writing to a signal, which is error-prone.

Because the hook runs after Angular has already checked the parent's bindings, so changing a value that the parent template reads makes the dev-mode second pass see a different value.

Example: a child sets parent.title = 'Loaded' in ngAfterViewInit. The parent header was rendered as "Loading" a moment before; the verification pass reads "Loaded" and throws NG0100. Fix by setting the value earlier (ngOnInit), using a signal or computed, or restructuring so data flows down only.

Use the constructor only for wiring (dependency injection and simple field setup); use ngOnInit for work that needs the inputs.

In the constructor, normal @Input values are not set yet, so this.userId is undefined; in ngOnInit they are ready. The constructor also runs in unit tests and server-side rendering the same way, so keep it free of HTTP calls and DOM access. With signal inputs you can read them in a computed or effect instead of waiting for a hook.

No. Mutating an array (push) keeps the same reference, so ngOnChanges does not fire.

Angular compares the bound value with ===. If the parent does items.push(4), the child's input still points at the same array, and neither ngOnChanges nor an OnPush check is triggered. Replace the array instead: items = [...items, 4]. With signals, items.update(a => [...a, 4]). Only ngDoCheck would see the mutation.

code.title: NG0100: dev-mode verification pass

followUps:
Because the verification pass doubles the work of every binding, which is a cost you do not want for real users, and it is only a debugging aid.

It exists to catch code that breaks one-way data flow. In production builds the second pass is removed, so the bug does not throw, but it is still there: the screen can silently show stale data (the earlier value) until the next change detection. That is why you must fix it even though production seems fine.

Signals tell Angular exactly when a value changes, and writing to one during rendering is flagged or schedules another clean pass instead of silently going out of sync.

A computed() is derived and cached, so it cannot be changed from the template and always agrees with its inputs. If an effect or a child writes a signal that a parent view already read, Angular marks that view dirty and re-renders it. Writing signals inside computed is blocked outright, so the common causes of NG0100 largely disappear.

It means data moves in one direction only: from parent to child during checking, never back up.

Angular checks the root, then its children, in order. When a child is being checked it must not alter something a parent (already checked) displayed. Children report upward with events, which run outside the check. Example: parent shows count; the child may emit (add), the parent changes count in the handler, and the next cycle shows it. This makes one pass enough to reach a stable screen.

code.title: Pure pipe as a memoised function

followUps:
A pure pipe only re-runs when its input reference changes, and a mutated array keeps the same reference.

In the program above, list.push(0) does not change the array object, so the pure pipe returns its cached sorted result [1,2,3] and the 0 is missing. Fix: make an immutable update (list = [...list, 0]), or better, avoid the pipe and use sorted = computed(() => [...this.list()].sort()). Making the pipe impure also works but sorts on every change detection.

The async pipe subscribes to the Observable and calls markForCheck whenever a new value arrives, so an OnPush component updates correctly.

Without it, an OnPush component would ignore the emission because no input changed. The pipe also unsubscribes automatically when the component is destroyed. It is technically impure, but cheap because it just returns the latest stored value. In newer code you may convert the stream with toSignal() and read the signal instead.

Prefer a computed signal for values derived from component state, and a pipe for reusable formatting of a single value in templates.

A computed is cached, tracks its dependencies automatically and can be unit tested in the class: total = computed(() => price() * qty()). A pipe like fileSize converts 2048 into "2 KB" and is reused in many templates with different inputs. Filtering or sorting a list is derived state, so use computed; formatting a number or date for display suits a pipe.

code.title: Structural directive: TemplateRef and ViewContainerRef

followUps:
Inject TemplateRef and ViewContainerRef, and create the embedded view once per count when the input changes.

@Directive({ selector: '[appRepeat]' })
export class AppRepeat {
  private tpl = inject(TemplateRef);
  private vcr = inject(ViewContainerRef);
  appRepeat = input.required<number>();
  constructor() { effect(() => { this.vcr.clear();
    for (let i = 0; i < this.appRepeat(); i++)
      this.vcr.createEmbeddedView(this.tpl, { index: i }); }); }
}

The program above shows the same idea in plain JavaScript.

hostDirectives lets a directive or component include other directives on its own host element and re-expose selected inputs and outputs.

Example: a PrimaryButton component declares hostDirectives: [{ directive: Tooltip, inputs: ['tooltip'] }]. Every <app-primary-button tooltip="Save"> now has tooltip behaviour with no change to its template. It is composition instead of inheritance, and the host directives must be standalone.

Host bindings are declarative, work with change detection and server-side rendering, and avoid direct access to the raw DOM.

Writing host: { '[class.active]': 'on()', '(click)': 'toggle()' } lets Angular update only what changed and clean up the listener automatically. Direct nativeElement.style.color = 'red' breaks on the server (no DOM), can be a security risk with innerHTML, and bypasses Angular's tracking. If you must touch the DOM, use Renderer2.

Because each lazy-loaded module creates its own child injector, and providers listed in that module are registered there, separate from the root.

If OrdersModule lists CartService in providers and is lazy loaded, it gets a new CartService with empty state, while the rest of the app uses the root one. Result: two carts. Fix by using providedIn: 'root' in the service, and do not repeat it in lazy module providers.

It is provideRouter(routes), placed in the providers of bootstrapApplication.

bootstrapApplication(App, {
  providers: [provideRouter(routes, withComponentInputBinding())]
});

Features are added through with... functions instead of a configuration object. RouterModule.forChild corresponds to a nested routes array loaded with loadChildren. The same provide... naming is used for HttpClient, animations and others.

importProvidersFrom lets a standalone app register the providers of an existing NgModule, without importing the whole module into a component.

Example: importProvidersFrom(HttpClientModule, TranslateModule.forRoot()) inside the providers array of the bootstrap config. It is meant for older libraries that only ship as modules. For libraries that provide a provideX() function, use that instead because it is simpler and tree-shakable.

code.title: Signals: only dependents re-run

followUps:
Because OnPush only checks a component when an input's reference changes, and a mutation leaves the reference the same, so Angular thinks nothing changed.

Parent does user.name = 'Bo': the child's [user] input still holds the identical object, the check is skipped and the screen shows the old name. Replace the object, user = { ...user, name: 'Bo' }, or hold it in a signal and call set. Immutable updates make OnPush reliable and cheap.

markForCheck marks this component and its ancestors to be checked in the next cycle, while detectChanges runs change detection on this view right now.

Use markForCheck after changing state outside Angular's knowledge in an OnPush component (for example in a plain callback); it is cheap and safe, and Angular will run the check itself soon. detectChanges is synchronous and only for this component and its children, so calling it repeatedly is expensive and can cause errors during destroy. Prefer signals, which need neither.

Anything that relied on Zone.js to trigger a check after async work stops refreshing the screen unless it notifies Angular.

For example setTimeout(() => this.count++, 1000) on a plain field no longer updates the template. Fix: make count a signal (count.update(c => c + 1)) or call markForCheck. Third-party libraries that update state in callbacks may need the same care. Tests using fakeAsync and tick also change, so run them before switching.

The main risk is service instances being duplicated or lost when providers change scope, so you must check where each service is provided.

Moving a provider from a lazy module into the root gives one shared instance where there were two; the reverse gives each route its own copy. Also watch forRoot() modules, interceptors (order matters), and InjectionToken values. Add a test that checks a key service is the same instance where expected, and migrate one feature per PR.

Show measurable value in small steps, not a big rewrite: bundle size, build time, bugs, and how long onboarding takes.

I would first run one automated schematic on a low-risk feature, record the numbers (for example, build time down from 90 s to 40 s after esbuild), and share them. Then propose a time-boxed plan, such as 10 percent of each sprint, with no feature freeze. Pointing out that Angular 12 no longer receives security fixes is a strong, concrete argument for managers.

As an assistant for the repetitive parts, with every change reviewed and tested by a person.

AI can explain breaking-change notes from ng update, draft tests for components before migration, convert odd templates the schematic skipped, and summarise large diffs for review. It should not run unattended on production code and can invent APIs, so I would keep the official schematics as the main tool and check AI output against the Angular docs and the test suite.
